I'll work through each draft chapter carefully, applying the gate test to every candidate sentence.

---

**Ch 007 Draft — Candidates**

*"'My union, Tuppence, my union! It does not permit me to work before 11 a.m.'"*
The source has a line before this: Tommy applauds, gets told off, and Tuppence says "Dash it all, Tommy, we've got to *do* something for our money." Tommy then makes his union quip. In the draft the preceding beat is simply `"And now—to work!" she announced next morning.` then immediately the union line. The union quip is a *response* to her "we've got to do something" — but that triggering line is absent from the draft. Does a reader know what Tommy is responding to? He's saying his union won't let him work before 11 a.m. — that is self-evidently a comic dodge of her "to work!" call. A competent reader understands it as a humorous reply to the work announcement immediately above. Not confused — just less richly set up. **Not a finding.**

*"Tommy, you'll have something thrown at you."*
In the source, between the union line and this line, there is a further Tommy quip and Tuppence's "It's all very well for you to sit there being funny, Tommy. It would do you no harm to do a little brain work too." The draft cuts to "Tommy, you'll have something thrown at you" directly. The reader can see this as Tuppence's escalating threat — still parseable. **Not a finding.**

*"They repeated the wheeze ad lib; a couple of fruitless calls later—Tommy's impersonation had supplied many a Christian name and slammed many a door—they lunched briefly"*
The phrase "Tommy's impersonation had supplied many a Christian name and slammed many a door" is odd — in the source the *servant* shuts the door, and the successful calls supply Christian names; no door is "slammed" by Tommy's impersonation. But this is an internal compression artifact within the draft sentence; it is slightly awkward but the reader understands they made multiple calls using the voting-register ruse. Not genuinely confusing. **Not a finding.**

*"'And stifle this longing for vulgar sensation, Tuppence. It's a wonder Mr. Brown has not ere now done us to death.'"*
In the source, Tommy says this mid-lunch, with some context about the tour ahead. In the draft it is tacked onto "Then the Mayfair lady is clearly indicated" with no transition, making it appear to be part of the same speech. In the source these are two separate exchanges separated by Tuppence's despondency and Tommy's encouragement. However — a reader sees Tommy speaking, and the sentiment is self-contained. Slightly abrupt but parseable. **Not a finding.**

*"'Still, it is queer he hasn't wreaked vengeance upon us. We pass on our way unscathed,' she returned, and rose."*
In the source, after this exchange there is Tommy's self-deprecating "Perhaps he doesn't think us worth bothering about," Tuppence's indignant response, Tommy's walk-back, and then they rise. The draft cuts all of that and has Tuppence immediately rising after her line. This is an authorized compression of the lunch scene; it still parses. **Not a finding.**

---

**Ch 008 Draft — Candidates**

*"Tommy hesitated an instant, then dived into a telephone box. Tuppence was somewhere near South Audley Mansions; there was no time to find her."*
In the source, Tommy's reasoning is that he can't reach Tuppence and so calls Julius instead. The draft's "Tuppence was somewhere near South Audley Mansions" references where she was last seen — which was established in Ch 007 draft (they just came from South Audley Mansions together). Tuppence stayed behind while Tommy followed. That is clear from the prior chapter. Parseable. **Not a finding.**

*"Julius looked blank, then confessed: 'I guess I haven't more than three or four hundred dollars with me at the moment.'"*
In the source, Julius explicitly shakes his head — he looks as though he has no money — and Tommy's "face fell," *then* Julius confesses to having hundreds of dollars. The draft's "Julius looked blank" replaces the head-shake, and the reader understands the joke (apparent poverty → actually rich). No confusion. **Not a finding.**

*"Boris said, 'You are early. You have nearly half an hour.'"*

The source makes clear that Boris says this to Whittington, establishing that Whittington is traveling alone while Boris stays. That context is what prompts Tommy's reasoning about which man to follow. In the draft Boris's line is reproduced but the reasoning it triggers — Tommy realizing he must choose between them and deciding to phone Julius to cover Whittington — is elided. The *phone call* is retained, so the reader sees Tommy call Julius to cover Whittington, but there is no indication *why* Tommy can't simply follow Whittington himself. In the source the reason is explicit: he has almost no money after buying his own ticket, and Julius is needed to tail Whittington while Tommy stays on Boris. In the draft Tommy buys his own Bournemouth ticket (implied by "Whittington took a first-class single to Bournemouth" and then Tommy gives Julius "a ticket") but his reason for needing Julius is never stated.

Gate test: A reader sees Tommy immediately phone Julius to cover Whittington without understanding why Tommy, who is already at Waterloo, cannot simply board the train himself. Julius arrives, Tommy gives him a ticket (where did it come from?), and Tommy stays to follow Boris — but the draft gives no reason for this division of labor. The source's logic (Tommy is nearly broke, Julius has money; but more fundamentally Tommy bought a ticket and then decided to deploy Julius so he could follow Boris) is entirely absent. However — the ticket detail is present: Tommy gives Julius "a ticket," implying Tommy had already purchased one, and the reader can infer Tommy chose to stay for Boris. The money motive is cut but the action is clear enough. A competent reader would understand the split even without the explicit reasoning. **Not a finding.**

*"He went up and reproduced, as far as he was able, the peculiar knock."*
In the source, there is a full paragraph of authorial commentary: "What he ought to have done … What he did do was entirely foreign to the sober common sense which was, as a rule, his leading characteristic. Something, as he expressed it, seemed to snap in his brain. Without a moment's pause for reflection he, too, went up the steps…" The draft retains this paragraph intact and then says "He went up and reproduced, as far as he was able, the peculiar knock." This is fine — it is just the continuation of the action. **Not a finding.**

---

After applying all tests, I find **no valid structural findings** in either draft chapter. Every apparent seam either parses on its own for a competent reader, is a residue of an authorized cut, or is merely a less-ornamented version of the source.
